entries.basis: NONBLIND source adjudication of the three preserved opinions, not an additional blind vote. Both pages of the composer score inspected. All four staves remain in bass clef. The first cello opens on A4 (above the third upper ledger line), held across seven whole-note bars at quarter=55; later material includes further sustained upper-register writing and a short descending quarter-note gesture. Thus the level-2 opinion's claim that the first cello only reaches E4 is a genuine register-reading error: the physical cello demand is substantially higher. The two-minute span and almost entirely slow, stepwise or stationary material do not establish the whole-work technical variety of advanced/pre-diploma repertoire. Level 4 is a responsible early-advanced cello equivalent for exposed A4 control, shifting, tone and long crescendos. The quartet has a common slow pulse and mainly simultaneous chord changes; sensitive tuning and bow renewal are real demands but do not establish that coordination is harder than the upper cello part. Consequently no automatic whole-level ensemble uplift is applied. Level 3 is a plausible nearby lower estimate, while level 5 depends on the disputed uplift; the advisory 4 allows roughly one level of uncertainty.

sources.finding: Composer complete two-page notation: bass-clef first cello A4 at opening, quarter=55, sustained tied whole notes and later slow moving chords; not an E4 ceiling.
Primary work page identifies the original four-cello work, two-page composer score and approximately two-minute duration.

entries.basis: NONBLIND adjudication, preserving [4,5,6]. Actual composer score pages 1, 3, 6 and 8 inspected, covering opening motor writing, flowing middle material, central effects and final return. Opening quarter=170 eighths have repeated pitches and a stable shared pulse, so speed alone is not a pre-diploma argument. However first violin later sustains notes in the very high G6 region, with large changes back to ordinary register, while other parts carry motion; the ending again juxtaposes very high sustained notes with articulated/double-stop accompaniment. Bow-pattern changes, sul G, tremolo/sul ponticello, exposed high stopped-note placement and repeated high-to-low transitions together support level 6 for violin 1. The effects are manageable and the repetitive figuration limits the burden; no evidence supports a diploma grade or another ensemble uplift. Level 4 underweights the cumulative register demand; level 5 remains a reasonable adjacent estimate, not a demonstrated reading error. Final 6 reflects this work-specific combination rather than taking the highest opinion automatically. Coverage and performance choices leave about one level of uncertainty.

entries.basis: NONBLIND adjudication of [4,6,5]. Actual publisher opening preview inspected: Vivo quarter=120 in 3/4, basses 1 and 2 in treble clef, basses 3 and 4 in bass clef; top line uses off-beat entries, tied/slurred eighth-note gestures, chromatic inflection and upper register, with answering/displaced figures below. The treble-clef bass writing is a meaningful playing demand, but ordinary double-bass octave transposition must be respected: treble placement is not evidence of sounding violin-like heights. The first part is the more extended upper line. Level 5 is a defensible advanced-bassist advisory estimate for the register plus secure dance articulation, rather than mapping the publisher word intermediate directly to catalogue level 2. The whole-work publisher/composer context describes a playable intermediate quartet with rhythmic developments, supporting a bounded estimate despite later pages being unavailable. The level-6 opinion adds a level for groove and balancing upper parts; the visible coordinated, often parallel patterns do not demonstrate ensemble demands harder than the individual notes, so that uplift is not established. Level 4 is a plausible adjacent assessment rather than a proven clef error. Final 5 has approximately one-level uncertainty; full-work certification is not claimed.
